summary: Proposes a way to carry SMTP mail transfer over the virtual circuits provided by the X.25 network standard from CCITT.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains how an SMTP mail session can run directly on an X.25 virtual circuit. It specifies the call identifier, data handling, closing behavior, and useful timeout values.

questions: sending internet mail over x.25 networks
how does smtp work over x25
subtitle: Procedures for carrying SMTP sessions directly over X.25 virtual circuits.

tldr.problem: Earlier guidance suggested running a reliable end-to-end protocol over X.25 before SMTP, but the author reports that X.25 service had become reliable enough for direct use.
tldr.mechanism: One full-duplex X.25 virtual circuit carries each SMTP session, with a protocol identifier, ASCII data, and rules for resets, closing, and timeouts.
tldr.outcome: The author reports successful production use across public data networks in multiple countries and over private X.25 connections and LANs.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1090's status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo describes SMTP procedures for X.25 virtual circuits.

sections.title: One X.25 Circuit per Mail Session
sections.content:
RFC 1090 proposes a standard procedure for SMTP over the virtual-circuit facility of X.25. It revisits an earlier suggestion to use a reliable end-to-end protocol such as TCP over X.25, and says X.25 service was by then reliable enough for practical direct use.

One virtual circuit is opened for each SMTP session. Its full-duplex channel carries the session, and it is normally closed by the calling side. The author reports production use involving 24 public data networks in 22 countries, along with private X.25 connections and X.25 LANs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each mail session gets its own two-way X.25 connection. SMTP's commands and replies travel over that connection until it is closed.

sections.title: Call Data, Packets, and Closing
sections.content:
The first four octets of Call User Data should be protocol identifier C0F70000 in hexadecimal, though implementations should allow configuration per address. SMTP data may be split into packets as the sender prefers; sequences with the M bit set, up to 2048 bytes total, are encouraged. Q-bit and interrupt packets are unused and should be ignored.

On an X.25 level 3 reset, the virtual circuit should be cleared and the SMTP connection retried. Because X.25 discards packets in transit when the circuit is cleared, the calling side closes the SMTP session only after receiving the Service Closing message.
sections.plainLanguage: The call starts with a code that identifies this as the SMTP application. The client waits for the service's closing message before hanging up, because X.25 can discard data during a clear.

sections.title: Text and Timeouts
sections.content:
The data uses full ASCII-8 with no escapes or modifications. Lines end with CRLF; implementations should, if possible, also recognize LF alone. If call acceptance does not arrive within 100 seconds, or Service Ready within another 120 seconds, the call should be cleared and retried later.

After a session is established, the circuit should be cleared after 10 minutes without a response. After QUIT, the timeout is shortened to 20 seconds; the RFC notes that this can cause an ungraceful exit but does not affect completed SMTP transactions. Permanent virtual circuits and D-bit selection are not used.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo sets waiting limits for call setup, an idle session, and shutdown. It also specifies the character encoding and line ending used for SMTP text.
